title: Should you replace your roof before installing solar panels?
dek: If an asphalt roof is past about 10 years old, consider replacing it first, since removing and reinstalling panels later can cost $7,000 or more.
keywords: cost to remove and reinstall solar panels
how old can my roof be for solar
keyPoints: Solar panels typically produce power for 25 to 30 years. Asphalt shingle roofs usually last about 30 years; metal and tile can last more than 50.
EnergySage suggests considering a roof replacement first if an asphalt roof is more than 10 years old.
Removing and reinstalling panels later runs about $200 to $300 per panel, and total costs can pass $7,000.
Removing panels can void the panel manufacturer's warranty, so ask who does the work and how warranties carry over.
Get the roof inspected and get the roof answer in writing before you sign a solar contract.

sources.title: Should you replace your roof before adding solar panels? (EnergySage)

body: A solar system is built to sit on your roof for 25 to 30 years. If the roof under it needs replacing in year 8, the panels have to come off first and go back on afterward, and EnergySage puts that at about $200 to $300 per panel, with totals that can pass $7,000. That is why the age of your roof belongs in the solar decision from the start.

Here is the basic timing problem. Asphalt shingle roofs, the most common kind, usually last about 30 years. Metal and tile roofs can last more than 50. Solar panels typically keep producing for 25 to 30 years, and many keep going longer. A new array on a 20-year-old shingle roof means the roof will almost certainly wear out while the panels still have years of life left.

For example, take a 20-panel system. At $200 to $300 per panel, a remove-and-reinstall job would cost roughly $4,000 to $6,000 in that example, before any roof work, and larger systems or complicated mounts cost more. That money buys no extra electricity. It just puts you back where you were.

EnergySage's rule of thumb is to consider replacing an asphalt roof first if it is more than 10 years old. That does not mean every 11-year-old roof must go. A roof in good shape can have plenty of life left, which is why an inspection matters more than the number alone.
Step 1: Find out your roof's age and material. Look for the original roofing invoice, permit records, or home inspection report from when you bought the house.
Step 2: Get an independent roof inspection. A roofer who is not selling you solar can tell you how many years the roof has left and whether any section under the planned array needs repair.

Step 3: Ask each solar installer how they handle roofs. Some offer workmanship warranties covering the part of the roof where panels are mounted, often around 10 years. Ask what is covered, for how long, and who pays if a leak starts at a mounting point.

Step 4: Ask about future removal. Removing panels can void the panel manufacturer's warranty, depending on who does it. Ask the installer whether they offer removal and reinstallation, what they charge today, and whether doing it through them keeps the warranties intact.

Step 5: If you replace the roof first, coordinate the timing. Doing the roof right before solar avoids a second round of scaffolding and lets the roofer and installer plan flashing and mounting together.

What if the roof is fine but not new? Then the choice comes down to math. Compare the cost of replacing now against the likely remove-and-reinstall bill later plus the roof replacement you will need anyway. Some homeowners decide to replace only the roof sections that will hold panels; ask your roofer whether that makes sense for your house.
Your next step today: find your roof's installation year and write it on the same page as your solar quotes, so every installer has to answer the roof question before you compare prices.
